title: Operator latency surgery: observability playbook for tail-latency incidents
author: Sofia Alvarez
content:
Summary:
This playbook describes the "operator latency surgery" workflow: a focused, observable-first investigation and remediation procedure for stubborn tail-latency incidents in LLM inference stacks. It is intended for platform operators and on‑call engineers who need to diagnose and restore service latency SLOs (p50/p95/p99) while preserving throughput and cost constraints.

Scope and intent:
- Scope: production runtime services that participate in inference request paths (edge/ingress proxies, routing, batching, KV prefix cache, model runtime workers, GPU scheduler, and dependent infra such as redis/cassandra).
- Intent: give operators a repeatable prioritized checklist for fast detection, triage, mitigation, and post-incident learning. Emphasize safe mitigations (non-destructive), observability hygiene, and owner-driven RCA.

When to run this procedure:
1. Any p99/p999 token-latency SLO breach longer than 5 minutes.
2. User-facing latency degradation reported that affects multiple tenants or routes.
3. Sustained increase in tail latency without corresponding token-cost changes (suggests infra, not workload).

Pre-flight checks (first 3 minutes) — quick facts to gather:
- Which routes / model_ids are affected? (console request traces or route labels)
- Which regions and availability zones show symptoms?
- Is the degradation correlated with traffic spikes, background deploys, or scheduled maintenance?
- What SLOs are burning? p50/p95/p99 token latency heatmap.

Observable-first investigation (ordered, with PromQL/ES examples):
1) Confirm alert and scope:
   - Check SLO dashboard and traces. Look for sudden jumps in p95/p99 across: runtime_proxy, batcher, model_worker.
2) Heatmap of request categories by latency and token_count (Prometheus example):
   - PromQL: sum by(route,region)(histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[2m])) by (le, route, region)))
3) Check batching and queueing backlog:
   - PromQL: sum(rate(batcher_queue_size[1m])) by (queue_name, model_id) and histogram of batch sizes: rate(batcher_batch_size_sum[1m]) / rate(batcher_batch_size_count[1m])
4) Inspect kernel / runtime worker stalls and GPU scheduling:
   - Metric: model_worker_busy_seconds / model_worker_cpu_seconds_total, and gpu_scheduler_pending_jobs.
5) KV prefix cache and cold miss flood:
   - Query: rate(kv_cache_miss_total[5m]) by (cache_shard); check prefix miss amplification.
6) Downstream datastore latency (Redis/Cassandra):
   - ES/Kibana query: latency > 10ms for redis GETs in the last 5m, or cassandra read95 > 200ms.
7) Correlate with deploy/infra events:
   - Look at deployment change events, kernel upgrades, node reboots in the timeframe.

Quick decision matrix (on-call):
- If batcher queueing high & p99 up: prefer emergency batching cap reduction or route-level soft-queueing.
- If gpu_scheduler backlog with idle workers: check container placement and preemption logs.
- If kv_cache miss amplification: enable read-through cache warmup or limit tenant prefix eviction.
- If downstream datastore slow: route to degraded datastore tier or enable local fallback cache.

Safe mitigation recipes (apply in controlled order):
1) Traffic shaping (soft):
   - Apply route-level slow-down: increase sampling ratio for heavy routes, reduce max_tokens and max_input_length for degraded route. Example RPC: curl -X POST https://console.internal/api/route-configs/{route} -d '{"soft_quota":0.7}'
2) Batching caps:
   - Reduce max_batch_size on the batcher (non-destructive). kubectl patch deployment batcher --type=json -p '[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/env/0/value","value":"64"}]'
3) Circuit isolation:
   - Enable per-tenant circuit-breaker for noisy tenant IDs using the OPA policy gate. (See OPA policy examples below)
4) Model fallback:
   - Route to a compatible lower-latency quantized model variant with A/B fallback; flip traffic through the routing API with gradual steps (10% -> 50% -> 100%).
5) Operator hotfixes:
   - If kernel-level stalls suspected, trigger an operator-safe-cache-drop on the affected shard with the internal tool: /opt/bin/cachectl drop-shard --shard x --grace 30s

Alert tuning and recommended thresholds (table):
| Component | Metric | Example threshold (global) | Operator action |
|-----------|--------|---------------------------:|-----------------|
| runtime-proxy | request_duration_seconds p99 | > 1500ms for 5m | Run entire playbook / page oncall |
| batcher | batcher_queue_size | > 500 requests backlog | Reduce batching cap, disable elastic-batching |
| model_worker | model_worker_cpu_steal | > 10% over 5m | Investigate node preemption / GPU contention |
| kv_prefix_cache | kv_cache_miss_rate | > 1k misses/min | Warmup cache shards, lower eviction aggressiveness |
| redis | redis_avg_latency_ms | > 20ms p95 | Failover to read-replica, cache local copies |

Note: thresholds must be tuned by region and tenant tier; alert noise reduction is prioritized over aggressive global firing.

Example Prometheus queries (copy/paste):
- p99 by route: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, route))
- batcher backlog: sum(batcher_queue_size) by (region,queue)
- gpu pending: sum(gpu_scheduler_pending_jobs{state="pending"}) by (region)

Tracing and flamegraphs:
- Use the tracing console to inspect a set of slow traces (p99 samples). Key spans to inspect: runtime-proxy->batcher->kv-prefix-cache->model_worker->gpu-kernel. Export flamegraph of top 100 traces and look for repeated hot spans.

Operator commands and scripts (examples):
- Check pod restart and OOMs: kubectl get pods -l app=model_worker -o json | jq '.items[] | {name:.metadata.name, restarts:.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount}'
- Temporarily reduce batch size for a deployment: kubectl rollout restart ds/batcher --patch='{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"batcher","env":[{"name":"MAX_BATCH","value":"32"}]}]}}}}'
- Re-route traffic to fallback model: curl -X POST https://routing.internal/api/switch -d '{"route":"/v1/generate","variant":"quantized-v2","step":0.1}'

Post-mitigation verification: checklist (do not skip):
1. Confirm p99 has returned below threshold for 10 minutes.
2. Confirm token throughput is within expected bounds (no silent throttling).
3. Verify no increased error rates or hallucination regressions introduced by fallback models (run quick eval suite).
4. Collect conservative trace samples and persist a zipped artifact for RCA.

Post-incident actions and RCA template:
- Owner: assign a 3-person RCA team (owner, telemetry lead, infra lead).
- Timeline: produce an initial RCA within 48 hours and a mitigation roadmap within 7 days.
- RCA should include: root cause hypothesis, evidence (graphs, trace excerpts, CLI logs), corrective actions, and preventive work items (dashboards, alerts, platform changes).

Observability hygiene and instrumentation improvements (recommended):
- Tag requests with tenant_id, route, model_variant, model_version, and token_count at ingress.
- Emit batcher-level histograms (batch_size, wait_ms) and instrument KV cache hit/miss with prefix labels.
- Add a lightweight synthetic p99 canary per region that runs a 32-token generation every 30s.

Owner and escalation contacts:
- Primary oncall: platform-operators@redwood.internal (pager)
- Secondary: runtime-infra@redwood.internal
- Observability engineering owner: Priya Nambiar (priya@redwood.internal)

Appendix A — OPA policy example (snippet):
# allow request when tenant score < limit
package routing

default allow = false

allow {
  input.tenant_score < 0.8
}

Appendix B — Example artifact collection checklist:
1) Export Prometheus query results (CSV) for key metrics 30m before and after mitigation.
2) Save 50 p99 traces (trace IDs) and aggregate flamegraphs.
3) Collect kube events, node kernel logs (dmesg), and GPU host logs for affected nodes.
4) Archive batcher and model_worker logs for the incident window.

Appendix C — Related dashboards to check:
- Service overview: runtime p50/p95/p99 by route and model_variant
- Batcher internals: queue size, batch size distribution, latency per batch
- KV prefix cache: miss heatmap by shard and tenant prefix
- GPU scheduler: pending queue, preemption events, device saturation

Maintenance and review cadence:
- Run a quarterly "latency surgery" game day: recreate noisy-tenant and datastore slow scenarios in the synthetic lab.
- Maintain an annual review of alert thresholds following traffic growth and new model variants.

Document owner: Sofia Alvarez (platform observability) — update this playbook when we add new routing primitives or when SLO definitions change.
